summary: Specializing in Buddhist studies and philosophy, Kosen Imakita studied at Sōgen-ji, Shokoku-ji, and under Togai Fujisawa, Shoen Daisetsu, Gisan Zenkai, and Kyokuso Hirose. He served as abbot of Eikō-ji and Engaku-ji, and as a doctrinal instructor in the Ministry of Religion.
Specializing in Indology and Buddhist studies, Koshin Suzuki completed doctoral studies at Taisho University, where he also served as a researcher (attested 1995–1998).

Koshiro Tamaki worked in Buddhist studies, philosophy, and Indology, earning his doctorate from the University of Tokyo. He held posts at Toyo University, served as a professor at the University of Tokyo (1964–1976), and held professorships at Tohoku and Nihon universities.

Focusing on Buddhist studies and Indology, Kosho Kawamura studied at Toyo University under Giyu Nishi, Nichijin Sakamoto, Shunkyo Katsumata, Koshiro Tamaki, and Yoshiro Tamura. He served as an assistant, lecturer, and full-time researcher at Toyo University, later lecturing at Minobusan and Hamamatsu.

Specializing in Buddhist studies, Kosho Mizutani studied at Ryukoku University and earned a doctorate from Bukkyo University. He served as an associate professor and later president of Bukkyo University (1979–1989), and headed Bukkyo Kyoiku Gakuen and Tokai Gakuen.
Kosho Murakami worked in the fields of Buddhist studies and religious studies, having studied under Kodo Sawaki and Hideki Yukawa.
Active in Buddhist studies, Koshu Itabashi studied at Sendai Daiichi High School, the Imperial Japanese Naval Academy, and Tohoku University (~1950–1953) under Teruji Ishizu.

Specializing in Buddhist studies, Kosuke Nakazawa served at the Institute for the Comprehensive Study of Lotus Sutra (attested 2001) and held appointments at Rissho University as professor (attested 2001) and professor emeritus (attested 2026).

Focusing on Buddhist studies and Indology, Kotatsu Fujita studied at the University of Tokyo and Harvard University under supervisors Shoson Miyamoto and Hajime Nakamura, among others. He was a professor at Hokkaido University (~1969–1986) and former president of Sapporo Otani Junior College.
A scholar in Buddhist studies, Kotetsu Yoshida is attested in 2014 as an adviser at the Kawasaki Daishi Research Institute of Buddhist Studies and professor emeritus at Taisho University.
Koun Kajiyoshi was a scholar in Buddhist studies who studied at the University of Tokyo (~1925–1928) and held a post at Taisho University.
Working in Buddhist studies and history/archaeology, Koyo Sakaino held posts at Toyo University (~1900–1933) and Komazawa University (~1904–1933).
A scholar in Buddhist studies, Koyo Shimizu studied under Shoko Takeuchi and was an adjunct lecturer at Ryukoku University (attested 1995).

Focusing on Buddhist studies, Koyu Tamura completed his master's and doctoral degrees at the University of Tokyo. He held posts at Nishogakusha University and Toyo University, where he became associate professor in 1972 and professor emeritus in 1977–2000.

Kozen Shaku worked in Buddhist studies and Indology, studying under Senmyō. He served as abbot at Gyokuri-ji (1870–1881) and Sannei-ji (1882), and taught at Nagano Prefectural Northern Chugakurin (1881).

Active in Buddhist studies, history/archaeology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies, Kozui Otani studied at Gakushuin and Kyoritsu Gakusha under Eun Maeda. He served as the 22nd Abbot of Nishi Hongan-ji (1903–1914).
An Indologist, Krishna Kamal Bhattacharya studied at Sanskrit College and Presidency University. He later held positions at Presidency University (1862–1872) and Surendranath College (1891–1903).

Indologist Krishna Kanta Handique earned master's degrees from the University of Calcutta and the University of Oxford, also studying in Paris and Berlin. He served as Principal of Jorhat College (1930–1948) and Vice-Chancellor of Gauhati University (1948–1957).

Working in Indology and linguistics, Krishna Mohan Banerjee studied at Hare School, Presidency University, and Bishop's College under Alexander Duff. He served on the faculty at Hare School (~1829–1832) and as Second Professor at Bishop's College, Kolkata (1852).

Krishna Venkateswara Sarma worked in Indology and history/archaeology, studying at the University of Kerala under V. A. Ramaswami Sastri. He held key posts at Panjab University, served as director of the Vishveshvaranand Vedic Research Institute, and headed the K. V. Sarma Research Foundation.
